```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
    collapse = TRUE,

    eval = FALSE

```

This vignette describes how to go from structural variant (SV) assemblies to a
reconstructed neo-chromosome Hi-C map. The assembly file format is the one
produced by [NeoLoopFinder](https://github.com/XiaoTaoWang/NeoLoopFinder)
`assemble-complexSVs`.

## 1. Get SV assemblies from NeoLoopFinder

NeoLoopFinder expects a six-column SV list:

```text
chr7    chr14   ++      14000000        37500000        translocation
chr7    chr14   --      7901149 37573191        translocation
```

The columns are:

1. `chrA`: chromosome of the first breakpoint.
2. `chrB`: chromosome of the second breakpoint.
3. `orientation`: `++`, `+-`, `-+`, or `--`.
4. `b1`: first breakpoint position on `chrA`.
5. `b2`: second breakpoint position on `chrB`.
6. `type`: `deletion`, `inversion`, `duplication`, or `translocation`.

Then run `assemble-complexSVs`, for example:

```bash
assemble-complexSVs \
    -O SKNMC \
    -B SKNMC-EagleC.SV.txt \
    --balance-type CNV \
    --protocol insitu \
    --nproc 6 \
    -H SKNMC-MboI-allReps-filtered.mcool::resolutions/25000 \
       SKNMC-MboI-allReps-filtered.mcool::resolutions/10000 \
       SKNMC-MboI-allReps-filtered.mcool::resolutions/5000
```

This produces `SKNMC.assemblies.txt`. A typical file looks like this:

```text
A0  inversion,8,132915000,+,8,130825000,+   deletion,8,130800000,-,8,129520000,+    8,132155000     8,129375000
A1  inversion,11,84315000,-,11,83565000,-   inversion,11,84315000,+,11,83565000,+   11,85050000     11,82625000
C0  translocation,1,10260000,+,X,21495000,- 1,9380000       X,22205000
C1  translocation,1,10260000,-,X,21495000,+ 1,10630000      X,20080000
```

## 2. Understand the assembly file format

Each non-empty line is one assembly:

```text
<assembly_id> <SV records...> <span1> <span2>
```

The fields are tab-separated:

- `assembly_id`: a unique ID such as `C1`, `A0`, or `C16`.
- `SV records`: zero or more SV records, each formatted as
  `type,chrA,b1,strandA,chrB,b2,strandB`.
- `span1`: the first assembled span, formatted as `chr,position`.
- `span2`: the last assembled span, formatted as `chr,position`.

The SV records and spans define the ordered nodes of the neo-chromosome:

```text
span1 position
  -> SV1 chrA position
  -> SV1 chrB position
  -> SV2 chrA position
  -> SV2 chrB position
  -> ...
  -> span2 position
```

Consecutive node pairs become fragments. A fragment is marked as flipped when
its entry position is greater than its exit position. For example:

```text
C1  translocation,12,65690000,-,14,68280000,+   12,66455000   14,67645000
```

This gives:

| fragment | chromosome | interval | orientation |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | chr12 | 65690000-66455000 | flipped |
| 2 | chr14 | 67645000-68280000 | flipped |

`readNeoAssembly()` reproduces this topology, applies optional end extension,
and assigns cumulative `offset` and `length` values in the concatenated
neo-chromosome.

```{r read-assembly, eval=FALSE}
library(plotgardener)

neo <- readNeoAssembly(
    file = "HM1_merged.assemblies.txt",
    id = "C1",
    assembly = "hg38",
    extend = 200000
)
neo
neo$fragments
```

### Custom assembly files

You can also create an assembly file yourself. It must contain at least one
tab-separated line with an ID, the SV record(s), and the two spans:

```text
C1  translocation,1,0,-,2,0,+   1,400   2,400
```

Here `chr1:0-400` is reverse-complemented and `chr2:0-400` is forward, giving a
400 bp + 400 bp neo-chromosome.

### Chromosome names and coordinates

- `readNeoAssembly()` adds a `chr` prefix when it is missing. Set
  `prefix = ""` if your data uses unprefixed names.
- Positions are used as supplied. `.hic` readers are 1-based and `.cool`
  readers use 0-based bin starts; plotgardener handles the source-specific
  bin starts when mapping.
- `extend` adds bases only to the first and last fragments, matching the
  common NeoLoopFinder visualization convention.

## 3. Reconstruct the neo-chromosome matrix

`readNeoHic()` reads each fragment pair from a `.hic`, `.cool`, or `.mcool`
file and maps the contacts into neo-chromosome coordinates.

Use the exact normalization column stored in the file. For NeoLoopFinder
workflows, this is often `sweight` (from `correct-cnv`) or `weight` (ICE):

```{r read-neohic, eval=FALSE}
neo <- readNeoAssembly(
    file = "HM1_merged.assemblies.txt",
    id = "C1",
    extend = 200000
)

neoHic <- readNeoHic(
    data = "HM1_merged-Arima-R1-filtered.mcool",
    neo = neo,
    resolution = 5000,
    norm = "sweight"
)

neoHic
head(neoHic$matrix)
```

You can also pass the assembly file and ID directly:

```{r read-neohic-path, eval=FALSE}
neoHic <- readNeoHic(
    data = "HM1_merged-Arima-R1-filtered.mcool",
    neo = "HM1_merged.assemblies.txt", id = "C1",
    extend = 200000, resolution = 5000, norm = "sweight"
)
```

`readNeoHic()` also accepts a precomputed genomic pair data frame with
columns `chrom1`, `start1`, `chrom2`, `start2`, and `counts`:

```{r read-neohic-df, eval=FALSE}
neoHic <- readNeoHic(
    data = pairData, neo = neo,
    resolution = 5000
)
```

Check the available columns with:

```{r norms, eval=FALSE}
readCoolNorms(
    "HM1_merged-Arima-R1-filtered.mcool",
    resolution = 5000
)
```

The reconstruction keeps bins in the coordinate space but drops contacts whose
normalization weight is missing or non-finite, matching the usual NeoLoopFinder
visualization behavior.

## 4. Plot the reconstruction

```{r plot-neo, eval=FALSE}
pageCreate(width = 5.5, height = 6, default.units = "inches",
           showGuides = FALSE)

hicPlot <- plotNeoHic(
    neoHic,
    type = "triangle",
    x = 1, y = 0.9, width = 3.4, height = 1.9,
    just = c("left", "top"),
    zrange = c(0, 0.005),
    palette = colorRampPalette(c("white", "#FFDFDF", "#FF7575",
                                 "#FF2626", "#F70000"))
)

## Solid outer neo-chromosome domain + dotted internal seams
annoNeoDomains(hicPlot, neo)

## Fragment backbone with directional arrows
plotNeoAssembly(
    neo,
    x = 1, y = 3.05, width = 3.4, height = 0.16,
    just = c("left", "top"),
    fill = "#D4EEF9",
    labels = TRUE,
    show.seams = TRUE
)
```

For more control over fragment labels, turn labels off in the backbone and use
`annoNeoFragmentLabels()`:

```{r neo-labels, eval=FALSE}
plotNeoAssembly(
    neo,
    x = 1, y = 3.05, width = 3.4, height = 0.16,
    just = c("left", "top"),
    labels = FALSE
)
annoNeoFragmentLabels(
    neo,
    x = 1, y = 3.3, width = 3.4,
    label.style = "coordinate",
    label.position = "below",
    label.offset = 0.05,
    label.fontsize = 7,
    label.fontface = "italic",
    label.fontcolor = "black",
    show.inversion = TRUE,
    inversion.color = "red"
)
```

`annoNeoFragmentLabels()` supports chromosome, coordinate, or fragment-number
labels, custom fonts/colors/rotation, vertical offsets, and inversion marking.

`annoNeoDomains()` is the functional equivalent of the dotted seam/domain
annotations in the NeoLoopFinder triangle examples:

- outer domain outline: solid, controlled by `lty`
- internal fragment seams: dotted, controlled by `seam.lty`

## 5. Map genes and other features

`mapNeoFeatures()` maps BED-like data or a `GRanges` object into the
neo-chromosome coordinate system:

```{r map-features, eval=FALSE}
genes <- data.frame(
    chrom = "chr12",
    start = 65822483,
    end = 65968291,
    name = "HMGA2",
    strand = "+"
)

mapNeoFeatures(genes, neo)
```

For features that span a fragment boundary, the feature is split across
fragments. Strand is inverted for reverse-complemented fragments.

## 6. Practical notes

- Use a resolution that gives a reasonable number of bins across the
  neo-chromosome. `resolution = "auto"` targets roughly 1,000 bins.
- For NeoLoopFinder, run `correct-cnv` first if you want `sweight`
  normalization.
- If your `.cool`/`.mcool` chromosome names lack `chr`, either add the prefix
  as recommended by NeoLoopFinder or let `readNeoAssembly()` add it to the
  assembly side and use `readCoolNorms()` to verify the file side.
- `readNeoHic()` uses the existing `readHic()`/`readCool()` readers, so the
  raw contact extraction is the same as for ordinary plotgardener Hi-C plots.
